risk_rationale: A simultaneous deterioration in labor demand (NFP +29K, down 86K from prior), a 54bp surge in 10Y yields to 4.96%, and a 61bp widening in HY OAS to 340bp signals a material tightening of financial conditions that is beginning to bite the real economy. Oil at $107.9 WTI / $115.2 Brent adds a stagflationary overlay that complicates the Fed's path. The combination of slowing growth, sticky inflation above target, and tightening credit is the most adverse macro configuration for risk assets.
outlook_headline: Financial conditions are tightening faster than the economy can absorb — labor, credit, and housing are all cracking simultaneously.
outlook_body: Real GDP growth of 2.2% annualized provides a thin buffer, but the leading indicators are deteriorating sharply: NFP collapsed to 29K, HY spreads blew out 61bp, and the 10Y yield hit 4.96% — a level that is mechanically crushing housing and leveraged credit. Core PCE at 3.0% and Core CPI at 2.6% keep the Fed from pivoting, trapping policy in a stagflationary bind where easing risks re-accelerating inflation and holding risks a hard landing. The saving rate at 4.1% and rising credit card delinquencies (2.9%) suggest the consumer buffer is thinning. PMs should position defensively: the probability of a policy error — in either direction — is elevated and rising.

tabs.gdp: Q3 real GDP growth of 2.2% annualized is above stall speed but is a lagging read; the forward-looking data — NFP at 29K, HY spreads at 340bp, and mortgage rates at 7.32% — point to a meaningful deceleration ahead. The primary downside risk is a consumer-led slowdown as credit tightens and the labor market softens faster than wages can compensate. A sub-1% GDP print in the next quarter is a credible base case if current financial conditions persist.
tabs.jobs: NFP of +29K is a near-recessionary print, down 86K from the prior reading and well below the ~100K threshold needed to absorb new labor force entrants. This is not noise — it is consistent with the credit tightening, rate shock, and oil-driven margin compression visible across the dashboard. Leading indicators (HY spreads, mortgage applications, ISM employment sub-indices) suggest further deterioration; the labor market is transitioning from a lagging support to an active headwind.
tabs.unemp: U-3 unemployment at 4.2% remains historically low but is a lagging indicator that will follow the NFP trend with a 2-3 month lag. The U-6 underemployment rate at 7.6% — a 181bp gap above U-3 — signals meaningful slack in hours worked and part-time-for-economic-reasons, which is not captured in the headline. This breadth of labor market softness is inconsistent with the Fed's full-employment mandate being met and will accelerate if NFP prints remain sub-50K.
tabs.wages: Wages at 3.9% YoY remain above the Fed's implicit ~3.0-3.5% comfort zone for a 2% inflation target, but the real wage gain against CPI of 3.7% is essentially zero (+0.2pp). Workers are not accumulating real purchasing power, which constrains consumption durability even as nominal wages look resilient. The wage-price spiral risk is diminishing, but wages are not decelerating fast enough to give the Fed confidence to ease.
tabs.cpi: Headline CPI at 3.7% YoY is running 170bp above the Fed's 2% target, with the gap between headline and Core CPI (2.6%) of 110bp almost entirely attributable to energy — WTI at $107.9 is a direct upside risk to headline re-acceleration. Core CPI at 2.6% is trending in the right direction but remains above target; any oil-driven second-round effect into transportation and goods would reverse recent progress. The Fed cannot declare victory on inflation with this configuration.
tabs.pce: Core PCE at 3.0% is the Fed's preferred gauge and is 100bp above target — this is the number that keeps the FOMC on hold or biased hawkish regardless of labor market softness. The personal saving rate of 4.1% is low by historical standards, indicating consumers are drawing down buffers to sustain spending against real wage stagnation and higher debt service costs. PCE headline at 3.4% will be sensitive to any further oil pass-through, making the inflation outlook binary around energy price trajectory.
tabs.yield: The 10Y yield surging 54bp to 4.96% is the single most consequential move on the dashboard — it represents a sharp tightening of financial conditions that is not Fed-driven but market-driven, likely reflecting term premium re-pricing and fiscal supply concerns. The 10Y-2Y spread at +31bp is technically positive but the curve re-steepening is occurring via a bear steepener (long end selling off faster), which historically is associated with stagflationary regimes, not benign recoveries. The Fed at 3.88% Funds rate is now 108bp below the 10Y, meaning the market is doing additional tightening work — but this also raises the risk of an overshoot.
tabs.credit: HY OAS widening 61bp to 340bp is an alert-level move that signals deteriorating risk appetite and rising default expectations in leveraged credit. IG OAS at 89bp remains contained but will follow HY if the labor market deterioration accelerates and earnings guidance weakens. At 340bp, HY is not yet at distressed levels (typically 500bp+), but the velocity of the move — 61bp in one snapshot — is the warning sign; momentum in spread widening tends to be self-reinforcing as CLO and loan fund outflows accelerate.
tabs.housing: The 30Y mortgage rate at 7.32% — up 95bp from the prior snapshot — is a severe affordability shock layered on top of already-stretched home prices; at this rate, the monthly payment on a median-priced home consumes an historically high share of median household income. Housing Starts at 1,221K show the market has not yet fully capitulated, but permit data and builder sentiment will deteriorate with a lag as the rate shock is absorbed. The 1.93% YoY Case-Shiller HPI gain (up 127bp from prior) is a lagging artifact — expect this to reverse sharply as transaction volumes collapse under 7.32% mortgage rates.
tabs.oil: WTI at $107.9 and Brent at $115.2 represent a significant supply-side inflation shock that directly threatens the Fed's ability to declare disinflation progress. At these levels, energy is adding approximately 100-150bp to headline CPI and PCE on a sustained basis, and trucking, airline, and manufacturing input costs are rising — creating second-round inflation risk. This is the most stagflationary input on the dashboard: it simultaneously raises inflation, compresses consumer real income, and slows growth.
tabs.banks: Rising credit card delinquencies at 2.9% and a near-recessionary NFP print are early warning signals for bank consumer credit books, particularly in unsecured lending and auto. Net Interest Income (NII) tailwinds from the rate environment are partially offset by higher funding costs as the 2Y yield sits at 4.65% and deposit betas continue to reprice. The HY spread widening to 340bp will pressure mark-to-market on leveraged loan portfolios and reduce new issuance fee revenue; banks with heavy CRE exposure face compounding risk from 7.32% mortgage rates suppressing transaction activity and valuations.

signal_flags.note: A 54bp surge in the 10Y in a single snapshot is a financial conditions shock. Bear steepening at this magnitude historically precedes either a policy response or a credit event. Transmission into mortgages, corporate borrowing costs, and equity discount rates is immediate and severe.

61bp of spread widening in one period is a risk-off signal of high conviction. While 340bp is not yet distressed, the velocity matters — forced selling in loan funds and CLO reinvestment slowdowns can create non-linear spread dynamics from here.

A 29K print is borderline recessionary and the 86K sequential decline is not mean-reversion noise. If confirmed by next month's data, this will shift the Fed's reaction function and trigger a significant repricing of the soft-landing narrative.

A 95bp move in mortgage rates in one snapshot is an extreme affordability shock. At 7.32%, housing transaction volumes will collapse, builder margins will compress, and wealth-effect support to consumption will reverse. This is a systemic drag on Q4 and Q1 growth.

Oil at $107.9 WTI / $115.2 Brent is a stagflationary input that prevents Fed easing while simultaneously slowing growth. Any further supply disruption pushing WTI above $115 would materially worsen the inflation outlook and increase recession probability.

The HPI uptick is a lagging data artifact — it reflects transactions closed before the 95bp mortgage rate surge. Forward-looking housing data will deteriorate sharply; do not interpret this as housing stabilization.
